Hashmi was a strong supporter of the Virginia Clean Economy Act (SB 851, 2020), which set Virginia on a path to 100% renewable electricity by 2045. Hashmi voted to repeal Virginia's Marshall-Newman Amendment (SJ 29, 2020), which had constitutionally banned same-sex marriage, and supported replacing it with language affirming the right to marry regardless of sex. Hashmi opposed Republican bills in the VA Senate that would have restricted transgender students from participating in sports aligned with their gender identity. As chair of the Virginia Senate Education and Health Committee, Hashmi blocked multiple Education Savings Account (ESA) and school voucher bills from advancing, including HB 1508 (2023). Hashmi patroned legislation creating a Child Care Workforce Development Fund to subsidize training and wages for early childhood educators and consistently advocated for expanded child care subsidies. Hashmi co-patroned the Virginia Dream Act, which restored in-state tuition eligibility for DACA recipients, and opposed omnibus immigration enforcement cooperation bills. Hashmi supported limiting Virginia law enforcement cooperation with ICE detainer requests and backed sanctuary-supportive legislation. Hashmi championed Medicaid expansion implementation and sponsored multiple healthcare equity bills during her VA Senate tenure. She co-patroned legislation expanding maternal health coverage and advocated for universal coverage, framing healthcare as a right throughout her campaigns and senate career.

Hashmi voted for the Virginia Clean Economy Act (2020) mandating the phase-out of fossil fuel electricity generation by 2045 and opposed bills that would have weakened Dominion Energy's clean energy transition timeline. She backed offshore wind development as a clean alternative to continued fossil fuel reliance.

Hashmi was a co-patron of legislation establishing no-excuse absentee voting in Virginia (2020) and supported automatic voter registration through the DMV. She opposed all voter ID restriction bills and supported restoring voting rights for returning citizens with prior felony convictions.

Hashmi supported the 2020 Virginia constitutional amendment creating an independent redistricting commission (SJ 18), which passed with bipartisan support. She backed measures to ensure the redistricting process includes community input and protections for minority voting power, consistent with her civil rights advocacy.

Hashmi supported legislation requiring more detailed disclosure of large campaign contributions in Virginia and backed efforts to close disclosure loopholes for dark-money affiliated organizations. She has called for stronger campaign finance transparency in her capacity as a senator and as Lt. Governor candidate.

Hashmi supported progressive tax measures during her VA Senate tenure, including budget provisions that increased corporate income tax contributions to fund education and Medicaid. She backed expansion of the Virginia earned income tax credit for working families and consistently favored tax policies that address economic inequality.

Hashmi supported police reform legislation without endorsing defunding. She co-patroned legislation establishing a statewide law enforcement use-of-force database (2020 special session) and supported requiring body cameras for state law enforcement. She distinguished reform from abolition, emphasizing community safety investment alongside accountability.

Hashmi supported legislation reforming mandatory minimum sentences for certain drug offenses in Virginia (2020 special session) and co-patroned bills expanding parole eligibility. She framed criminal justice reform as an equity issue, noting racially disparate incarceration rates, and backed the 2021 marijuana decriminalization and legalization legislation.

Hashmi voted to ban chokeholds by Virginia law enforcement (2020 special session) and co-patroned the creation of civilian law enforcement review boards. She supported stronger whistleblower protections for officers who report misconduct and called for robust independent oversight of police departments.

Hashmi supported legislation banning source-of-income discrimination in rental housing and backed the Virginia Housing Trust Fund expansion in multiple budget cycles. She co-patroned bills to increase affordable housing funding and supported statewide zoning reforms to allow accessory dwelling units.

As Virginia's first Muslim state senator, Hashmi has spoken about protecting religious practice in public life while opposing religious exemptions that enable discrimination. She opposed legislation that would create religious liberty exemptions for businesses to discriminate but supported protecting employee religious accommodation rights in workplaces. Her approach balances protecting personal religious expression without allowing it to override civil rights protections.

Hashmi was a strong advocate for Medicaid expansion implementation in Virginia, supporting full funding and eliminating administrative barriers. She backed expanding Medicaid coverage for postpartum care and consistently supported preserving and expanding federal Medicare coverage in all budget deliberations.

Hashmi supported economic development tied to workforce equity and inclusive growth. She backed workforce training programs and co-patroned legislation to fund workforce development in underserved communities. She also supported broadband expansion initiatives as an economic development tool for Virginia communities.

Hashmi was the primary patron of SJ 2 (2024), the Virginia Reproductive Freedom Amendment, which placed abortion rights in the state constitution. In her first term she voted for SB 1318 (2020) and HB 1090 (2020) to expand abortion access in Virginia, and she consistently earned 100% ratings from NARAL Pro-Choice Virginia. She has called abortion access "fundamental healthcare" in floor speeches.

However, he has historically had lower ACLU ratings than MA delegation peers (60-70%) and was a late convert on same-sex marriage. He opposed some LGBTQ+ rights measures in his earlier career. His civil rights positions reflect his South Boston Catholic Democratic background — generally supportive of racial equality but more conservative on LGBTQ+ issues historically.

Lynch is a practicing Catholic who has at times cited religious values in his positions on abortion. He has been more cautious about religious exemptions in the LGBTQ+ context than most MA Democrats, reflecting his Catholic constituency in South Boston. He voted for the Equality Act but has been less vocal in opposing religious liberty arguments than progressive colleagues. He represents a classic blue-collar Catholic Democrat position on religious freedom.

Lynch has one of the most conservative abortion records of any Massachusetts Democrat. He voted for the Stupak-Pitts Amendment (2009) which would have banned abortion coverage in the ACA exchange plans. He opposed the Women's Health Protection Act and has historically received low ratings from NARAL (25-40%) while earning scores from anti-abortion groups. He has described himself as a Catholic who opposes abortion. In the 2013 MA Senate special election primary against Ed Markey, his anti-abortion record was a major issue. He has not been a cosponsor of abortion rights legislation.

Lynch has not taken a highly visible public position on transgender athlete inclusion in sports. He voted against the Republican Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act (2023) but has not been a vocal advocate for transgender inclusion. His conservative Catholic background and moderate record on LGBTQ+ issues over the years suggests a more cautious middle position. He supported the Equality Act's overall non-discrimination framework.

Garcia's public safety record is mixed: as Long Beach mayor he received criticism from activists for his financial ties to the Long Beach Police Officers Association union, yet he also championed community programs and proposed ballot initiatives for ethics oversight. As a congressman he has not called for defunding police; his Progressive Caucus affiliation suggests support for adding crisis response teams without reducing core police funding.

As Long Beach mayor Garcia's administration converted hotels into transitional housing and expanded shelter capacity as the primary homelessness response strategy. The city operated outreach programs and service connections. While the city enforced some public-space rules, Garcia's stated priorities centered on shelter expansion and services rather than enforcement-first approaches.

Garcia introduced a Universal Basic Income proposal for foster youth exiting the system ($1,000/month for 5 years) and is a Progressive Caucus member that opposes criminalizing public sleeping. As mayor he invested in shelter capacity and transitional housing conversions. He supports decriminalizing public presence and redirecting resources toward service connections rather than criminal penalties.

Wikipedia documents that Garcia voted in favor of three military aid supplemental packages for Ukraine, Israel, and Taiwan in April 2024, alongside most Democrats. This reflects continued support for Ukrainian defense at current levels without committing to dramatically expanded aid or unconditional escalation.

Garcia is co-chair of the Congressional YIMBY Caucus, which co-introduced the People Over Parking Act (eliminating parking minimums) and the Build More Housing Near Transit Act — both signaling strong support for multimodal transportation investment over car-centric infrastructure. He sits on the House Transportation & Infrastructure Committee's Highways and Transit subcommittee.

Garcia committed Long Beach to the Long Beach College Promise (free college pathways) and set a goal of universal preschool enrollment — both representing investment in public education institutions. He is a member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which strongly opposes voucher programs that divert taxpayer money from public schools to private institutions.

Garcia is a founding member of the Congressional Freethought Caucus, which is dedicated to maintaining the secular character of government and opposing religious exemptions that override civil rights protections. He supports LGBTQ non-discrimination laws without carve-outs. The Freethought Caucus explicitly backs the Johnson Amendment barring political endorsements by tax-exempt religious groups.

Garcia is a member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which advocates for significantly higher taxes on wealthy individuals and corporations to fund social programs. He co-founded Mayors 4 Medicare (2020) and committed Long Beach to universal preschool — both requiring progressive revenue sources. His public statements consistently frame taxation as a tool for funding public goods.

Garcia represents CA-42 (Long Beach), home to the largest US container port; he has consistently opposed broad tariffs that threaten port trade and jobs. As Long Beach mayor he established international trade relationships with Asia, Europe, and Latin America, signaling a pro-trade posture. As a Progressive Caucus member he supports selective environmental tariffs but not sweeping protectionist tariffs.

As mayor of Long Beach, Garcia proposed and passed a ballot initiative (Measure BBB) creating an independent redistricting commission for the city — removing elected officials from the process. His membership in the Congressional Progressive Caucus aligns with support for independent non-partisan redistricting nationally.

Garcia co-sponsored the Stop Ballroom Bribery Act (Nov. 2025) with Sen. Warren to ban presidents from accepting private donations for White House renovations and imposing a 2-year lobbying ban on contributors — targeting dark-money corruption at the executive level. As a Progressive Caucus member he has consistently backed strong donation limits and disclosure requirements.

OnTheIssues records Garcia as opposing Social Security privatization. He co-founded Mayors 4 Medicare (2020) to advocate universal healthcare access. In March 2026 the Congressional Progressive Caucus — of which Garcia is a member — announced joint opposition to Republican proposals to cut Social Security benefits and healthcare coverage.

As Long Beach mayor, Garcia actively pursued international trade partnerships and city economic development while requiring Project Labor Agreements with construction unions — demonstrating a targeted-incentives approach with labor quality requirements. He recruited businesses while demanding community benefit conditions such as green certifications and worker retention plans.

As mayor of Long Beach, Garcia announced a goal of universal preschool enrollment and committed the city to the Long Beach College Promise — both reflecting a policy of significantly expanding publicly supported early childhood access. His Progressive Caucus membership aligns with federal investment in childcare subsidies and provider grants for low- and middle-income families.

Crighton supported the 2022 millionaires surtax (Question 1) and the 2023 tax relief package. He has consistently supported progressive taxation and opposed regressive tax structures. He has backed the Child and Family Tax Credit expansion and tax relief measures targeted at working families and renters. He has voted against tax cuts that primarily benefit high-income earners and supported state tax policy that funds essential services in lower-income communities like Lynn.

Edwards supported the 2022 millionaires surtax (Question 1) and has backed progressive taxation as a means to fund services for her constituents. She has backed the Child and Family Tax Credit and tax relief measures for renters and lower-income residents. She has consistently voted for progressive budget priorities and supported using the surtax revenue specifically for affordable housing, education, and transportation in underserved communities.

Fernandes supported the 2022 millionaires surtax (Question 1) and has backed progressive taxation. He has advocated for using surtax revenue specifically for housing and environmental infrastructure on Cape Cod. He has backed the Child and Family Tax Credit and has supported tax policy that funds essential services for year-round residents rather than vacation homeowners. His tax approach emphasizes ensuring working Cape Cod residents benefit from state tax policy.

Feeney supported the 2022 millionaires surtax (Question 1) and has consistently backed progressive taxation to fund public services and worker protections. His union background informs his view that progressive taxation ensures wealthy corporations and individuals pay their fair share while protecting services for working families. He has backed the Child and Family Tax Credit and opposed tax policies he views as disproportionately benefiting corporations over workers.

Lewis supported the 2022 millionaires surtax (Question 1) adding a 4% surcharge on incomes over $1 million for education and transportation. He has consistently backed progressive taxation and opposed tax cuts that primarily benefit high earners. He supported the 2023 tax relief package while also advocating that its benefits be weighted toward lower- and middle-income residents rather than across-the-board cuts. He has backed increasing the minimum wage and expanding the earned income tax credit.

Jehlen strongly supported the 2022 millionaires surtax (Question 1) and has consistently backed progressive taxation. Keenan supported both the 2022 millionaires surtax (Question 1) and the 2023 tax relief package. DiDomenico supported the 2022 millionaires surtax (Question 1) and the 2023 tax relief package. Driscoll supported both the 2022 millionaires surtax (Question 1) and the 2023 tax relief package. Brownsberger supported the 2022 millionaires surtax (Question 1) and the 2023 tax relief package. Davis's campaign advocates connecting transit expansion (TRAX and FrontRunner) with affordable housing to prevent resident displacement, describing transit access as a community asset. Montigny voted for the 2022 VOTES Act making expanded mail voting and early voting permanent. His approach to public safety is more balanced between reform and traditional policing than some progressive colleagues, reflecting his ward constituency's priorities.

Strezo has supported Somerville's HEART program and community-based public safety alternatives, while also emphasizing the importance of adequate traditional police services for public safety. She backed mental health crisis response expansion and police accountability measures, including civilian oversight. Her stance balances reform and community investment with maintaining police capacity for traditional public safety functions.

Wilson has supported community-based public safety alternatives and backed the Somerville HEART program (Holistic Emergency Alternative Response Team), a civilian-led crisis response program that deploys mental health workers instead of police for certain 911 calls. He was involved in advancing this initiative as a state legislator and has expanded it as Mayor. He has backed police reform measures including civilian oversight of use-of-force policies while also maintaining he supports adequate police staffing for traditional public safety functions.

Ewen-Campen co-authored the resolution creating Somerville's HEART (Holistic Emergency Alternative Response Team) civilian crisis response program and has been its strongest champion on the council. He backed expanded police accountability measures, civilian oversight, and reforms to use-of-force policies. He framed the 2020 police reform debate in terms of structural reallocation toward community investment and was one of the most outspoken council members for reducing police budgets and expanding alternative services.

Sait, as a social worker by background, has been one of the strongest advocates on the council for community-based public safety alternatives. She was an early and vocal champion of the HEART program and has pushed for expanded mental health services and social services as primary responses to non-violent emergencies. She has backed police accountability reforms and viewed over-policing as a racial equity issue, supporting reallocating police funding toward social services and mental health crisis response.

Clingan has supported the HEART program and community-based public safety alternatives on the Somerville City Council, backing mental health crisis response and police accountability measures. He has voted with the council majority on reform-oriented public safety measures while maintaining a balanced approach that also recognizes traditional policing needs in his ward. His stance reflects support for reform with continued police capacity for serious crime response.

Mbah supported the creation and expansion of Somerville's HEART program, advocating for mental health crisis response as an alternative to police response for non-violent emergencies. He also championed civilian oversight of the Somerville Police Department and pushed for anti-racial profiling policies. He was an early supporter of police accountability reform following the 2020 racial justice movement and has consistently backed community investment as a crime prevention strategy over enforcement-first approaches.

Link has supported Somerville's HEART (Holistic Emergency Alternative Response Team) civilian crisis response program and backed expanding mental health services as a public safety alternative. He has expressed support for community-based violence prevention approaches and has backed civilian oversight of policing. His public safety stance emphasizes diverting calls that do not require police response to trained civilian responders while maintaining adequate traditional public safety capacity.

Mayor Davis-Holmes has supported a dual-track approach to homelessness in Carson combining encampment clearances under Los Angeles County Homeless Initiative protocols with coordinated referrals to county shelter and services. She has publicly stated that Carson residents deserve clean public spaces and expressed support for LAHSA outreach teams deployed to Carson encampments along the I-405 and Dominguez Channel corridors. While backing enforcement of anti-camping ordinances, Davis-Holmes has also advocated for increased county funding for shelter beds serving the South Bay and pointed to housing affordability as a root cause requiring state-level action. This combined enforcement-and-services approach places her at a centrist position on the homelessness-response spectrum.

Mayor Davis-Holmes has been a vocal advocate for workforce development and local hiring in Carson's industrial and logistics sector, supporting the city's partnerships with Amazon and other distribution center employers to provide jobs for Carson residents. She championed a local hiring preference policy requiring large logistics employers near the I-405 corridor to give first-look opportunities to Carson-area residents, framing economic development as a tool for community benefit rather than simply attracting businesses. Davis-Holmes has also supported the Dignity Health Sports Park (former StubHub Center / Cross Campus) as an anchor for broader South Bay economic development and has backed city-sponsored small business assistance programs.

Mayor Davis-Holmes has supported maintaining Carson's contract with the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department for law enforcement services while also advocating for community-oriented policing programs and youth diversion efforts. She backed the city's LASD station funding in multiple budget cycles and has spoken publicly about the need for adequate patrol staffing in Carson's neighborhoods. At the same time, Davis-Holmes has supported the city's gang intervention and youth violence prevention programs as complementary to law enforcement. Her public safety record reflects a mainstream center position — supporting the LASD contract while also emphasizing prevention and community engagement alongside traditional policing.

Mayor Davis-Holmes supported Carson's 2022 Housing Element update to comply with the state's Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) requirement of approximately 2,000 new units, embracing state affordability mandates rather than contesting them as some neighboring cities did. She has publicly backed streamlined ADU (accessory dwelling unit) permitting as a practical tool for adding affordable housing stock in Carson's established neighborhoods and supported affordable housing set-asides in new mixed-use developments in the city's commercial corridors. Davis-Holmes has cited the need for housing near the Dignity Health Sports Park and the city's Amazon logistics employment centers as reasons to facilitate new residential construction.

Mayor Davis-Holmes supported placing a local utility user tax (UUT) measure on the ballot to help fund city services in Carson, framing additional local revenue as necessary to maintain public safety staffing and infrastructure maintenance given the city's historically lean general fund. She backed the city's existing utility tax structure and opposed proposals to reduce it without identifying replacement revenue. Davis-Holmes has also supported county and state tax measures benefiting cities, including Measure H funding for homelessness services. Her tax record is moderately progressive — supporting targeted local tax measures for services rather than across-the-board cuts.

Mayor Davis-Holmes has supported new mixed-use development and infill projects in Carson's commercial corridors, particularly along Carson Street and near the Dignity Health Sports Park, as tools for job creation and housing supply expansion. She backed the city's effort to redevelop underutilized industrial and commercial parcels with projects combining affordable housing, retail, and community amenities. Davis-Holmes endorsed a community benefits agreement framework for larger developments, requiring prevailing-wage construction jobs and set-asides for Carson residents. Her growth positions lean toward welcoming development when it includes community benefits rather than strict preservation of existing land uses.

Mayor Davis-Holmes has supported Carson's alignment with LA County's immigrant-protective policies, including limiting voluntary cooperation between the city's contracted LASD station and federal immigration enforcement beyond what California law requires under the TRUST Act and VALUES Act. She backed a Carson City Council resolution affirming the city's commitment to its immigrant community and opposing ICE enforcement operations that targeted working-class Latino and other immigrant communities. Davis-Holmes has publicly characterized immigration enforcement tactics as disruptive to Carson's diverse community and economic life.

Mayor Davis-Holmes has advocated for improved transit access in Carson, supporting bus rapid transit improvements along the Metro Silver Line (Harbor Transitway) serving the South Bay and backing Measure M-funded transit investments in the I-405 corridor. She has spoken at South Bay Cities Council of Governments (SBCCOG) meetings in favor of increased bus service frequency on Metro routes serving Carson's predominantly transit-dependent residential areas. Davis-Holmes backed protected pedestrian and bicycle infrastructure improvements in Carson's commercial corridors as part of Complete Streets planning. Her transportation positions lean toward transit investment and multi-modal access over auto-only infrastructure.

Dunleavy opposes relaxing immigration laws and has strongly backed enforcement-first immigration policies, opposing the end of Title 42 expulsions and opposing pathways to citizenship for undocumented residents. His documented positions support deporting those without legal status, prioritizing enforcement, though no specific mass-deportation regardless of ties statement was found.

Dunleavy criticized Medicaid expansion as a legislator, questioning whether it is something to "be proud of" that one-third of Alaskans rely on Medicaid. He opposed ObamaCare expansion and has focused on helping Alaskans find private health insurance. He did sign an extension of postpartum Medicaid coverage but his overall record favors partial privatization and reduced government health program reliance.

Dunleavy has stated his goal is to help Alaskans "find health insurance without government assistance" and opposed ACA/Medicaid expansion. As a legislator in 2018 he questioned whether one-third of Alaskans on Medicaid "is something we should be proud of." He expanded postpartum Medicaid coverage to 12 months but his overall position is that government should play only a limited safety-net role.

Dunleavy opposes relaxing immigration laws and has characterized refugee resettlement without thorough vetting as a "hasty, poorly thought-out" policy. He opposed the Biden administration's termination of Title 42 border expulsions in 2022, calling it "detrimental to states." He supports strong immigration enforcement and no pathway to citizenship for undocumented residents.

Dunleavy is a strong fiscal conservative who declared "No change in taxes without a vote of the People," opposes higher taxes on wealthy individuals, and has opposed new broad-based taxes. He made $433 million in line-item vetoes in 2019 and consistently prioritizes spending cuts over revenue increases. His position aligns with cutting taxes across income levels.

Dunleavy has explicitly stated that "school choice is public schools, not private schools" (Jan 2025) and has focused on expanding charter schools and homeschool funding within the public system. He increased public homeschooling funding and signed the Alaska Reads Act. His position prioritizes public school funding while restricting choice to within the public system.

Dunleavy has declared his goal to make Alaska the "most pro-life state" and vetoed state-funded abortion appropriations in 2019. He proposed a constitutional amendment allowing Alaskans to vote on abortion protections, acknowledging competing views rather than seeking an outright ban with no exceptions, placing him at value 4 (restrict to rape/incest/serious health threat).

Dunleavy is a leading advocate for maximizing Alaska's fossil fuel extraction. He declared Alaska should "remain oil & gas giant for another 45 years," supported the Willow Project, Alaska LNG pipeline, Ambler Road, and opposed Biden-era drilling suspensions. He abolished the state climate task force and has pushed to remove federal restrictions on resource extraction.

Jehlen has been a strong healthcare access advocate who has championed the expansion of MassHealth and supported universal coverage approaches. She has backed the 2022 mental health parity law and legislation to improve access to mental healthcare for all residents. She has been a consistent advocate for reproductive healthcare access and supported measures protecting abortion rights. She has backed legislation improving access to gender-affirming care for transgender individuals.

Tarr has supported maintaining MassHealth coverage while raising cost-control concerns. He voted for the 2022 mental health parity law (Chapter 177) requiring insurers to cover mental health services equivalently to physical health. He has raised fiscal sustainability questions about Medicaid expansion costs and supported market-based approaches to lower prescription drug prices rather than government price-setting. His record reflects a centrist Republican position on healthcare: supporting access but opposing cost mandates on employers.

Brady has been a strong healthcare access advocate. Brockton is a community with significant healthcare needs and he has championed funding for Brockton hospital services, mental health treatment, and substance use disorder programs. He voted for the 2022 mental health parity law and has backed MassHealth expansion. He has also been a strong advocate for veterans healthcare, given the significant veteran population in his district. He has backed legislation improving access to behavioral health services and treatment for opioid addiction.

Lovely has been a strong advocate for healthcare access and mental health coverage. She voted for the 2022 mental health parity law (Chapter 177) and championed funding for substance use disorder treatment in Essex County. She has backed MassHealth expansion and supported legislation requiring insurers to cover opioid treatment. Her district includes Salem, a community significantly affected by the opioid crisis, and she has secured increased state funding for local treatment programs.

Lewis has been one of the most vocal state senators on expanding healthcare access. As Senate Chair of the Joint Committee on Public Health, he championed the 2022 mental health parity law and has been a strong advocate for universal healthcare coverage. He has backed legislation to study single-payer healthcare for Massachusetts and has consistently supported MassHealth expansion and protecting the ACA. He filed legislation to improve maternal health outcomes and has advocated for increased mental health funding throughout the state budget process.

DiDomenico has been a strong healthcare access advocate, particularly for children and families. His work on the Children, Families and Persons with Disabilities committee has included championing mental health services for children and expanding pediatric healthcare coverage. He supported the 2022 mental health parity law and has backed legislation improving access to behavioral health services. He has consistently voted for MassHealth expansion and healthcare access measures.

Cyr has been a strong healthcare access advocate throughout his career. He has championed rural healthcare access on Cape Cod and the Islands, where residents face geographic barriers to care. He backed the 2022 mental health parity law and has supported telehealth expansion to improve access for island residents. He has been a vocal advocate for LGBTQ+ inclusive healthcare and has backed legislation improving access to gender-affirming care. He has also championed HIV/AIDS prevention funding and supported MassHealth expansion.

Rodrigues has been a consistent healthcare funding advocate, using his Ways & Means position to prioritize healthcare in state budgets. He has backed MassHealth expansion and sustained funding for healthcare services in the South Coast region, which includes Fall River and New Bedford. He supported the 2022 mental health parity law and has backed substance use treatment funding. His district faces significant opioid and substance use challenges and he has worked to ensure treatment resources are available.

Voted YES on HB174 (Sex Characteristic Change Treatment Amendments, Feb 5 2026) passing 54-15, which permanently banned gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors. Snider appears in the official YES vote tally for this bill. Also voted YES on SB16 (2023) imposing a moratorium on gender-affirming hormone treatments for minors.

As House Majority Leader, operates within the Republican caucus that passed HB215 (2023) creating the $42 million Utah Fits All voucher program 54-20. Voted YES on HB467 and other Republican caucus priorities. Freedom index shows YES on HB116 (529 Plan Funding) for private education. No evidence he opposed the voucher program; conservative platform consistently favors school choice.

Snider was elected House Majority Leader in June 2025 and has voted with the Utah Republican caucus on all abortion-adjacent legislation. Voted YES on HB467 (2023) closing abortion clinics, and YES on HB467-related abortion restrictions. His freedom index record shows YES on closing abortion clinics (HB467, 2023). Utah's near-total trigger ban supported by Republican caucus. Has not sponsored pro-choice legislation.

Voted YES on HB106 (Income Tax Revisions, 2025) cutting Utah's income and corporate tax rate from 4.55% to 4.5% as part of $1.4 billion in cumulative 5-year tax cuts. His campaign platform emphasizes keeping taxes low and cutting government spending. Freedom index score of 77% reflects consistent support for tax reduction legislation.

Voted YES on HB226 (2025) requiring ICE coordination for immigrants convicted of violent crimes. As House Majority Leader, led the caucus that advanced multiple immigration enforcement bills during the 2025 session consistent with Trump administration deportation priorities. Freedom index shows YES on SB217 rejection (opposed CHIP for non-citizens).

Operates within Republican caucus that consistently favors enforcement-centered and shelter safety approaches to homelessness over expanded government services or housing-first policies. His conservative platform prioritizes limited government spending. Freedom index score of 77% reflects consistent votes with the Republican fiscal discipline approach.

Sponsored HB378 (2025) adding a new tax on wind and solar energy, and HB499 removing independent expert requirements from Utah's Air Quality Board. Also voted YES on SB57 (Utah Constitutional Sovereignty Act, 2024), asserting state authority to reject federal environmental directives. As a natural resources conservative he focuses on public lands extraction and opposes federal climate restrictions.

Said ICE "did have warrants" for people who "don't belong in this country" when defending immigration enforcement. Was the sole vote against the board's emergency declaration opposing ICE raids. Supports proactive cooperation with federal immigration authorities. Aligns with answer [4]: honor ICE detainers and share information proactively when federal agencies request it.

Endorsed the Gascón recall citing need for "maximum accountability" and victims' rights. Opposed lenient sentencing enhancements and stated soft-on-crime policies had "disastrous consequences." Primary focus is on deterrence and accountability for crime victims. Aligns with answer [4]: making sure others think twice before doing the same thing.

Barger's district transportation priorities are dominated by freeway and highway projects — including championing a $250M I-5 widening project and advocating for highway capacity expansion throughout the Antelope Valley and Santa Clarita. Transit investment is secondary. Aligns with answer [4]: focus on road capacity and traffic flow.

Barger describes enforcement as a "last resort" and prioritizes outreach, mental health services, and shelter placement. She opposed Governor Newsom's mass encampment clearance order as too blunt. Aligns with answer [3]: invest in outreach, shelter, and mental health services while enforcing reasonable public space rules.

Barger has stated "no rent cap should exist at all" and has repeatedly voted as the lone dissenter against tenant protection measures. Her district (Santa Clarita, Antelope Valley) is predominantly a homeowner/Republican constituency. Aligns with answer [5]: oppose rent control entirely; rents should be set by the market.

Provided an additional $1M in LASD funding in her district and was the sole vote against a motion to divert 10% of the police budget to social services. Consistently champions more deputies and law enforcement resources. Aligns with answer [4]: increase police staffing, equipment, and pay to improve response times and deter crime.

Voted with the full board to make LA County a "safe haven" for abortion access. Received endorsement from Planned Parenthood. Unusual for a Republican, her abortion stance reflects her moderate position in a heavily Democratic county. Aligns with answer [2]: keep abortion legal and accessible through the second trimester.

Davis's platform emphasizes community safety as a 'non-political' issue and calls for supporting 'survivors of violence' and treating all community members with dignity. Endorsed by Moms Demand Action, and her people-first framing is consistent with expanding shelter capacity and services as the primary strategy rather than criminalization as the first tool.

Davis's platform calls for treating 'immigrant families with dignity' and frames immigrant communities as integral to District 40. Endorsed by the SLC Democratic Party Black Caucus and SLC Labor Caucus, which have opposed mass deportation policies. Her stance is consistent with limiting deportation to serious violent offenses while protecting long-term residents and working families.

Davis explicitly frames immigrant families as part of the District 40 community and calls for treating them with dignity 'rather than fear,' signaling opposition to proactive local enforcement of federal immigration law. Her endorsement from the SLC Democratic Party Black Caucus and advocacy against fear-based enforcement are consistent with refusing ICE detainers and protecting undocumented residents.

Davis's platform prioritizes reducing Wasatch Front air emissions by 50% by 2033 and her endorsement from Green Wave Utah signals opposition to expanded fossil fuel extraction. Framing air quality as a health crisis is consistent with stopping new fossil fuel permits rather than merely maintaining current levels, though she has not explicitly called for an outright ban on all new drilling.

Davis's campaign platform explicitly states 'public dollars stay in public schools,' directly opposing diversion of public education funding to private institutions. Endorsed by IBEW Local 354 and UFCW Local 99 (labor unions traditionally opposing vouchers), with 10+ years of PTA involvement in the Canyons School District reinforcing her public education commitment.

Davis's platform includes backing Utah's goal to 'reduce Wasatch Front air emissions by 50%' from 2017 levels by 2033, addressing wintertime inversions as a health hazard. This supports clean energy investment and gradual emissions reduction but stops short of calling for an immediate fossil fuel phase-out or emergency declaration. Endorsed by Green Wave Utah (an environmental advocacy PAC), reinforcing a pro-environment stance.

Davis campaigns on the principle that 'when working people do well, the whole community does better,' endorsing organized labor representation in policy decisions, prevailing wage standards on public projects, and pricing transparency. Her union household background and labor endorsements (IBEW Local 354, UFCW Local 99, SLC Labor Caucus) indicate strong support for taxes that fund public services and worker protections rather than tax cuts.

Barr signed the First Amendment Defense Act protecting faith-based opposition to same-sex marriage and has consistently prioritized religious liberty over anti-discrimination protections. He opposes requiring religious groups to cover contraception or abortion in insurance and voted against barring federal contractors from discriminating based on sexual orientation.

Barr co-sponsored the Sugar Reform Act establishing import tariffs and marketing allotments to protect domestic sugar producers, reflecting selective protectionism for specific industries. The OnTheIssues profile notes he 'opposes expansion' of free trade and 'sponsored sugar quotas and import tariffs,' suggesting a mixed approach rather than blanket free trade or blanket protectionism.

Barr received a 0% rating from the Alliance for Retired Americans, indicating a pro-privatization stance on Social Security. He has supported prioritizing debt payments over Social Security in debt ceiling crises and has generally backed market-based reform over preserving the current guaranteed-benefit structure.

Barr voted for the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act and strongly opposes higher taxes on wealthy individuals. He supports a single-rate (flat) tax system, capital gains reductions, and complete repeal of the death tax 'with no expiration.' He signed the Contract from America backing constitutional limits on tax increases requiring a two-thirds majority.

Barr strongly supports coal production and offshore drilling, signing the No Climate Tax Pledge and opposing any restrictions on fossil fuel extraction. He withdrew an Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez invitation over concerns about the Green New Deal's impact on coal mining. His OTI profile documents strong opposition to green energy prioritization.

Barr signed the Contract from America opposing earmarks and supporting fiscal discipline, and his general record aligns with reducing campaign finance restrictions. He has not supported major disclosure or contribution limit legislation and his philosophy favors less government regulation of political speech and spending.

Barr disputes the scientific consensus on climate change, arguing 'Some say the science is settled. That's not true,' and signed the No Climate Tax Pledge. He opposes carbon tax implementation and invited backlash over the Green New Deal's coal impacts. His record reflects rejection of climate policy in favor of economic growth.

VoteSmart records Mrvan supporting entitlements (PVS survey, Sep 2020) and his Wikipedia page and available coverage indicate he backs Social Security expansion. His New Democrat Coalition membership paired with his pro-labor stance (co-sponsoring the PRO Act, endorsement by United Steelworkers) aligns with modestly increasing benefits while raising taxes on higher earners.

Mrvan is a member of the New Democrat Coalition, which supports a public option alongside regulated private insurance rather than single-payer. He opposed H.R.497 (the Freedom for Health Care Workers Act) in January 2023, which would have lifted vaccine mandates, showing support for public health regulation. His record reflects expanding affordable coverage through public programs and private insurance.

VoteSmart records Mrvan supports pathways to citizenship and opposes immigration bans based on religion (Apr 2021). He voted against H.J.Res. 24 allowing non-citizens to vote in D.C. local elections (Feb 2023). His overall posture is pro-legal-immigration while maintaining legal status distinctions.

As a New Democrat Coalition member, Mrvan supports maintaining and improving Medicare and Medicaid without pursuing full single-payer expansion. VoteSmart's PVS survey records him supporting entitlements. His NDC membership and voting pattern align with improving current programs while controlling costs rather than dramatic expansion or privatization.

Mrvan co-chairs the Congressional Steel Caucus and VoteSmart records him supporting 'Strong Buy America requirements and steel tariffs' (Jun 2022). His advocacy focuses on protecting key American industries like steel from unfair foreign competition — selective tariff use to defend domestic manufacturing jobs, not blanket high tariffs on all imports.

Mrvan sponsored legislation to expand voter registration and access in February 2021, certified the 2020 presidential election results in January 2021, and his VoteSmart profile records support for expanded voter access. This pattern aligns with expanding early voting and making mail-in voting available to all voters without requiring an excuse.

Mrvan cosponsored the Equal Rights Amendment deadline elimination (Mar 2021), co-sponsored the PRO Act (Protecting the Right to Organize Act), and is a member of the Congressional Equality Caucus and Black Maternal Health Caucus. His record reflects strengthening civil rights enforcement and addressing systemic discrimination across gender, race, and LGBTQ dimensions.

Council Member Lee voted in support of Alhambra's 2022 Housing Element Update, which rezoned dozens of parcels along Valley Boulevard and in commercial corridors to allow higher-density residential development in compliance with the state's 6th Cycle RHNA allocation of approximately 3,400 units. She expressed support for the plan as a way to address regional housing needs and avoid penalties from the state Department of Housing and Community Development. Her multi-term tenure coincides with the city's steady uptake of ADU-friendly policies and the removal of parking minimums in transit-adjacent zones.

Council Member Andrade-Stadler voted in favor of Alhambra's 2022 Housing Element Update, which rezoned parcels along Valley Boulevard and near commercial corridors to allow higher-density residential development in compliance with California's 6th Cycle RHNA allocation of approximately 3,400 units for Alhambra. The unanimous council vote to adopt the Housing Element was required to avoid state penalties from HCD for non-compliance. Her District 5 covers the southern portion of Alhambra where ADU expansion policies and transit-adjacent upzoning provisions also apply.

Council Member Wang voted in favor of Alhambra's 2022 Housing Element Update, which rezoned parcels along Valley Boulevard and near the Alhambra Multimodal Transportation Center to allow higher-density residential development in compliance with the state's 6th Cycle RHNA allocation of approximately 3,400 units. As Alhambra Council Member Wang (rotational Mayor 2025-26), she has continued to champion the city's RHNA compliance efforts and has publicly stated that meeting state housing mandates is necessary for Alhambra to avoid penalties from HCD. Her District 4 spans the northeastern residential area of Alhambra where several of the upzoned parcels are located.

Council Member Wang supported the 2022 Housing Element Update's rezoning provisions, which converted single-family and commercial parcels in several Alhambra corridors to allow multi-family and mixed-use development. She voted to adopt the plan's transit-adjacent upzoning overlay and the ADU expansion provisions that removed parking minimums near bus stops along Valley Boulevard. Her votes are consistent with California state law compliance on residential densification, reflecting pragmatic acceptance of state-mandated zoning changes rather than purely ideological upzoning advocacy.

As part of the 2022 Housing Element Update, Council Member Lee supported rezoning single-family and commercial parcels along Valley Boulevard and near the Alhambra Multimodal Transportation Center to allow mixed-use and multi-family development. The adopted plan included an "upzoning" overlay for transit-adjacent zones. Lee's vote to adopt the Housing Element represented support for allowing denser residential development in previously restricted zones, consistent with the state SB 9 and ADU frameworks.

Council Member Maza voted with the full Alhambra City Council to adopt the 2022 Housing Element Update, which committed the city to rezoning parcels to accommodate its state-mandated RHNA allocation of approximately 3,400 units for the 6th Housing Cycle. Maza stated during public discussion that housing production was a regional responsibility and that Alhambra needed to do its part under state law. His vote was in favor of the update, reflecting support for expanding housing supply through zoning changes and streamlined permitting.

Council Member Maloney voted with the full Alhambra City Council to adopt the 2022 Housing Element Update, satisfying the city's state-mandated RHNA obligation of approximately 3,400 new units for the 6th Cycle. During council discussion, Maloney acknowledged the state's housing mandate and the need for Alhambra to rezone sufficient capacity to avoid losing local land use control. His vote reflects support for state-compliant housing expansion as a practical necessity for the city to maintain autonomy over planning decisions.

Donahue supported the MBTA Communities Act multi-family zoning overlay for Waltham's transit station area, which modifies single-family and low-density residential zoning to permit higher-density multi-family development by right. His administration's submission of the compliance plan to the state signals support for expanding zoning to allow more housing types in previously restricted areas.

King voted in favor of Waltham's MBTA Communities Act zoning compliance plan in 2024, supporting the creation of a multi-family overlay district near Waltham's commuter rail station. As a multi-year at-large councillor, King has participated in votes on housing-related development projects and zoning matters. His vote to comply with MBTA Communities Act requirements reflects support for expanded housing production near transit.

LeBlanc voted in support of Waltham's MBTA Communities Act zoning compliance plan in 2024, which established a multi-family overlay district near Waltham's commuter rail station. As Council Vice President with a multi-year record, LeBlanc has participated in housing-related development votes and committee work on the Waltham City Council, generally supporting the majority position on housing production and zoning compliance.

Bradley-MacArthur voted in favor of the Waltham City Council's MBTA Communities Act zoning compliance plan in 2024, which created a multi-family overlay district near the city's commuter rail station to allow higher-density housing by right. The full Council's approval of the compliance plan, including Bradley-MacArthur's vote, signals support for expanding housing production near transit to address the regional affordability crisis.

Mayor Donahue led Waltham's compliance effort with the MBTA Communities Act in 2024, submitting a zoning amendment plan to create a multi-family overlay district near Waltham's MBTA commuter rail station. The Donahue administration presented the compliance plan to the City Council and supported its adoption to preserve Waltham's eligibility for state grants. This represents active support for new housing production near transit, placing him toward the pro-housing end of the scale.

Brasco voted in support of the Waltham City Council's approval of the MBTA Communities Act zoning compliance plan in 2024, creating a multi-family overlay district near Waltham's commuter rail station to permit higher-density housing by right. His vote as part of the full Council's approval reflects support for expanding housing production near transit corridors to address regional affordability challenges.

Laredo made housing affordability a central campaign issue in his 2025 mayoral race. He strongly supported Newton's compliance with the MBTA Communities Act, which requires zoning for multi-family housing near transit stops, and advocated for increased housing production throughout his time as a City Councillor. He has stated publicly that Newton must grow its housing stock to remain accessible to working and middle-class families.

Laredo has advocated for improved public transit and pedestrian safety in Newton, including support for better MBTA Green Line connectivity and safer bike infrastructure. His support for the MBTA Communities Act reflects a transit-oriented development philosophy. He has not articulated an aggressive car-restriction agenda but consistently favors transit and active transportation investment.

Laredo explicitly cited climate change action as a top priority during his mayoral campaign and first months in office. He supported the Newton Climate Action Plan as a City Councillor and has committed to accelerating the city's greenhouse gas reduction goals. He supports the state's Climate Act targets and Newton's building electrification work.

Laredo has supported a community-policing model and has backed Newton's unarmed mental health co-responder program. He has not advocated for defunding police but has expressed support for diverting some public safety calls to mental health professionals. This is consistent with the progressive-pragmatic approach common among Newton's elected officials.

Laredo supports managed economic and residential growth in Newton, backing the MBTA Communities compliance plan and transit-oriented development. He has expressed support for commercial development that generates tax revenue while prioritizing affordable housing inclusion. His approach is pro-growth but with equity and sustainability guardrails, typical of progressive suburban mayors.

Laredo named climate resilience and local environmental protection as top mayoral priorities. As a City Councillor he voted to advance Newton's Climate Action Plan, which set greenhouse gas reduction targets and committed the city to building electrification and renewable energy procurement. He has endorsed stronger tree canopy protections and green infrastructure investments.

Pressley voted for the Respect for Marriage Act (2022) and has been a strong supporter of LGBTQ+ equality throughout her career. She backed the Equality Act and consistently received 100% ratings from the Human Rights Campaign. She has spoken about LGBTQ+ rights as civil rights and has championed protections for LGBTQ+ youth in particular.

Pressley has civil rights as a central issue. She supported the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act, the Equality Act, and the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act. She has framed racial equity as the lens through which she approaches all legislation. She voted for H.R. 40 (Reparations Study Commission) and has been a leading voice for addressing systemic racism. She received perfect scores from NAACP and ACLU civil liberties scorecards.

Pressley fully supports transgender inclusion in sports consistent with the athletes' gender identity. She voted against the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act (Republican bill banning trans girls from female sports) and backed the Equality Act's comprehensive non-discrimination protections including sports participation. She has been among the most vocal congressional advocates for transgender youth and has framed trans exclusion as discriminatory.

Pressley supports religious freedom as an individual right while firmly opposing religious exemption claims used to justify discrimination against LGBTQ+ people and others. She voted for the Equality Act and has opposed RFRA expansions that could permit discrimination. She is a person of faith herself and has spoken about her religious values informing her social justice work, but she draws a clear line against using religion to harm others.

Pressley was one of few members of Congress to explicitly support divesting funds from police and investing in community safety alternatives. She backed the BREATHE Act and has consistently voted for the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act's strong accountability provisions. She has framed policing reform as a civil rights imperative and has called for community-controlled safety models. She has spoken about her own experiences with police violence in her community.

Pressley was one of the most vocal proponents of the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act including ending qualified immunity, national use-of-force standards, and civilian oversight boards. She has supported the BREATHE Act which called for defunding federal programs that support militarized policing. She has spoken at Black Lives Matter rallies and introduced legislation to end no-knock warrants federally. She has framed police accountability as the central civil rights issue of her generation.

Wicker is one of the strongest Republican supporters of Ukraine voting for every Ukraine aid package. In December 2021 he suggested considering preemptive military action against Russia and advocated for a no-fly zone over Ukraine. Schoen's own May 2025 Deschutes County voters' pamphlet statement says she will prioritize planning for growth, alongside fiscal responsibility and equitable access. Her recorded actions match: at the Sept. 23, 2025 BPRD meeting she made both motions to approve 20-year property-tax exemptions for the 98-unit Cascade Landing and 128-unit Verde Pines low-income housing developments and voted for both (each failed 2-2), accepting a calculated revenue loss to her own district so the housing could be built; and on July 21, 2026 she presented the City of Bend shared framework to the board as recognizing mutual benefit by supporting both housing and parks while avoiding actions that could compromise either agency's ability to deliver essential services, anticipating future work on SDC waivers, permitting, urban renewal impacts and transportation system fees. That is chair 3, 'Plan proactively - invest in infrastructure ahead of growth to support responsible expansion.' It is not chair 2, because she voted to enable the development rather than slow approvals until capacity caught up; and not chair 4, because she pairs support for new development with protecting the district's service delivery rather than reducing fees to grow the tax base.

Chair 2 ("strengthen civil rights enforcement and address systemic discrimination") rather than chair 3 ("maintain current civil rights laws while promoting equal opportunity"). The load-bearing evidence is LeGrand's own May 2025 Deschutes County voters' pamphlet statement, which under the heading "With your vote, I will continue to" pledges to "Promote equity-focused policies and student-centered programming" — a first-person, forward-looking commitment to enact equity policy, which is more than chair 3's maintenance of existing law. The same statement says "I bring expertise in equity, mental health, and inclusive programming." Context establishing which half of this topic's axis that equity language refers to (biography, not itself a stance): the listed occupation is "Professor, Afrocentric Program Coordinator" and the prior governmental experience includes the district's "Restorative Justice & Equity" role and the Oregon Department of Education "AABSS Advisory Group" (African American/Black Student Success) — i.e. the racial-inequality half. Not chair 1, which requires equity mandates across all institutions plus reparations; neither has been advocated. REVIEWER CAVEAT: this rests on a campaign pledge, not a policy record, and "promote equity-focused policies" carries no enforcement mechanism — a reviewer could defensibly argue chair 3. Resolution 1985 (Feb 11 2025, 7-0) is deliberately NOT cited as support: see wave6-school-z1-4-NOTES.md for why that resolution cannot discriminate chairs 2 and 3.

Chair 2 is 'strengthen civil rights enforcement and address systemic discrimination.' At the Deschutes County League of Women Voters candidate forum on 2025-04-23, reported by The Bulletin on 2025-04-24, Tomlin said in his own words: 'I fully support our DEI program at the district, and the right of these students to be learning in the classrooms.' The article also records that all three candidates present believed the district's plan to defend its diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives was a step in the right direction, and — in the reporter's own indirect speech, not a quotation — that Tomlin is looking forward to improving achievement gaps and working with underserved students. Independently, the official Deschutes County May 2025 voters' pamphlet statement furnished by Tomlin lists, under 'With your vote, I will continue to,' the commitment to 'Advance equity and inclusion' (attribution confirmed against the '(This information furnished by Ross Tomlin.)' block delimiter, since a neighbouring candidate uses the same heading). Explicitly endorsing an active district DEI apparatus — group-targeted remediation — at the moment the federal Education Department was pressing districts to end DEI goes beyond chair 3's 'maintain current civil rights laws while promoting equal opportunity,' whose framing is law-maintenance plus equal opportunity rather than an affirmative equity program. Chair 1 is excluded: nothing in the record calls for reparations or equity mandates across all institutions. REVIEWER CAVEAT: chair 3 is arguable, since 'fully support our DEI program' defends an EXISTING program rather than proposing to strengthen it.

In his own May 2025 Deschutes County voters' pamphlet statement Schneider commits to maximizing the impact of tax dollars by balancing reinvestment in existing parks with allocating appropriate resources for future growth, and to connecting trails and increasing park, green space and recreation-service capacity through thoughtful planning. Inferred from career pattern and platform framing — no single explicit quote addresses court access barriers, but the consistent pattern is unambiguous. Roy's entire campaign vision is built on eliminating barriers to legal access for workers, tenants, immigrants, and consumers who currently lack it. Her core platform commitment — stated consistently across all sources — is to make the City Attorney's Office "the largest public interest law firm in Los Angeles" (LAist, Patch, marissaroy.com). Her specific programmatic proposals are all access-maximizing: a dedicated "Tenants' Rights Team" to fight abusive landlords (SPNA), expanded wage theft investigation staffing, and using the office to pursue "workers, tenants, climate, civil rights" as top priorities (LAist). Her Patch Q&A describes bringing wage theft cases that "put thousands of dollars back in workers' pockets" — using government legal resources as a vehicle for those who could not otherwise afford representation against corporate defendants. Her career background — staff attorney at the Public Rights Project, consumer protection work at the California AG's office suing tech companies — embodies the value 1 framing: courts and legal resources exist for everyone, not just people with expensive lawyers. Low barriers mean more access to justice.

Roy's criminal justice philosophy is organized around breaking cycles of criminalization through evidence-based alternatives to incarceration. Her Patch Q&A states: "I want to pursue strategies that actually make our communities safer — one key goal is reducing recidivism, or the rate of reoffending. When we structure a public safety approach that breaks cycles of criminalization, we are preventing crime and making everyone safer." She explicitly describes diversion as connecting people to "behavioral health treatment, addiction support and counseling." Her LAist candidate survey states: "I would work to restore and scale up diversion programs, so we can use all of the tools in our toolbox to address public safety." Her campaign website frames the goal as "strategies that break cycles of criminalization, and make everyone in our communities safer." This maps to value 2: giving the person a fair chance to make things right through treatment, community service, or restitution. She is not at value 1 (pure rehabilitation focus) because she consistently frames outcomes in terms of community safety and explicitly maintains prosecution for cases requiring it — the goal is community safety through treatment, not rehabilitation as an end in itself.

Inferred from overall platform framing and career pattern — no single direct quote addresses the citizen vs. government deference question explicitly. Roy explicitly frames the office's primary obligation as being to the public — workers, tenants, consumers — against both corporate and city interests. Her campaign website states: "As City Attorney, I'll restore integrity to the Office to make sure our City Attorney serves the people, not the powerful." Her LAist candidate survey describes her mission as making the office the "most significant public interest law office in Los Angeles" to prioritize "workers, tenants, climate, civil rights." The LA Forward voter guide quotes her commitment to "holding abusive police accountable" and contrasts her with the incumbent's posture of defending city departments against misconduct lawsuits. Her proposed liability audit — inviting City Controller Kenneth Mejia to audit the office's settlement practices — signals that Roy sees independent review of city decisions as part of her mandate, not reflexive defense of city positions. Her entire career has been spent representing workers, tenants, and consumers against institutions (corporate and government) that have legal resources they lack. This places her at value 1: the citizen, almost always; government has lawyers, money, and power; regular people need courts to level the playing field.

Roy's approach to police misconduct liability combines accountability with smart settlement practice. The SPNA DTLA article identifies as a key platform element: "Critical of Incumbent: Her platform argues the current administration has spent too much on 'liability payouts' and has been overly aggressive in suing journalists and protesters." Her Patch Q&A states regarding legal liability: "For more long-term solutions, I'd work to bring departments in compliance with the law so that we prevent lawsuits before they occur" — framing LAPD compliance as a priority for reducing costs through accountability. The AOL/LA Times piece quotes her vowing "to put a particular focus on the Los Angeles Police Department, making sure it follows through on the recommendations drafted in the wake of costly litigation." Her proposed liability audit by City Controller Kenneth Mejia would scrutinize the office's existing settlement and defense practices for police-related cases. The LA Forward voter guide describes Roy as committed to "holding abusive police accountable" and contrasts her with the incumbent's posture of defending city departments against misconduct lawsuits. Roy's position — settle valid claims, make LAPD follow through on recommendations, audit existing practices — maps to value 2: settle valid claims quickly and pursue real accountability; defending misconduct wastes money and public trust. She does not reach value 1 (independent investigation against officials) because her emphasis is on smart liability management that produces accountability as a byproduct, not on the office acting as an independent police watchdog.

Hillier supports active but targeted economic development with job-quality strings attached. In her October 2024 candidate Q&A she advocated continued growth — "a city that sleeps eventually dies. We must always have an open eye for opportunity" — and highlighted the two urban renewal (tax-increment) zones the council created during her tenure, Basalt Creek (industrial/employment) and the downtown core, as examples of infrastructure development paired with "clean living wage jobs." Her emphasis is on specific districts and specific industry types with wage quality as the payoff, not maximal incentives for any employer; she has simultaneously prioritized reviewing codes and ordinances to remove unintentional barriers for development in those areas. That matches the targeted-incentives-for-specific-industries-with-job-quality-requirements chair rather than either refusing corporate incentives outright or treating recruitment of any large employer as the city's top priority.

Hillier's stated top priority for her second term is holistic long-range planning for Basalt Creek growth and downtown core development, with review of codes, ordinances, and zoning to eliminate unintentional barriers — planning proactively so the city shapes growth rather than reacting to it. In her October 2024 Q&A she embraced growth explicitly — "a city that sleeps eventually dies. We must always have an open eye for opportunity" — pointing to the Basalt Creek and downtown urban renewal areas where the city is front-loading infrastructure investment to support expansion. Nothing in her record supports growth moratoria or voter-approval gates, nor removing regulatory oversight entirely; she manages growth through long-range planning and infrastructure invested ahead of demand, the plan-proactively chair.

Bubenik has led an actively recruitment-oriented economic development program: under his mayorship Tualatin established two urban renewal (tax-increment) districts — the Southwest Basalt Creek Development Area for industrial/commercial employers and the Downtown Core Opportunity and Redevelopment Area — hired a dedicated urban renewal/economic development manager (Sid Sin), and committed $53 million to open 717 acres for employment development with new infrastructure, upsized utilities, and "additional incentive programs," with the Basalt Creek Manufacturing Park zone alone projected to accommodate ~1,897 new jobs. In March 2022 he identified the lack of developable land as among the city's biggest obstacles to economic growth, framing land supply for employers as a problem for the city to solve. This matches competing actively for major employers with significant incentives and infrastructure investment, though he balances it with small-business and Latino Business Networking support rather than treating growth as the city's sole priority.

Bubenik's posture is proactive planning and infrastructure investment ahead of growth: the city committed $53 million to open the 717-acre Basalt Creek/Southwest development area — Tualatin's first new investment area in over two decades — with new infrastructure and upsized utilities, and his 2025 State of the City promised "In 10 to 15 years, you'll see things going full-steam ahead" while highlighting the Transportation System Plan update nearing completion and two new urban renewal areas to shape industrial and downtown growth. As early as his May 2021 State of the City he was planning for buildout, noting "Tualatin will be built out except for infill unless we extend our boundaries." Nothing in his record supports growth moratoria or voter-approval requirements, nor wholesale removal of regulatory barriers; he manages growth through planning, annexation strategy, and front-loaded infrastructure.

Under Parris the city streamlined approvals (Prohousing Designation) and aggressively recruited major projects ($10B data centers, clean-energy industry) — a streamline-and-recruit approach.
Lancaster earned California's 2025 Prohousing Designation for streamlining development approvals and using city-owned land to spur housing — cutting regulatory barriers so housing gets built.

Inferred from council record and professional background: Hutchenrider explicitly advocated for adding fire station funding to potential 2026 bond priorities ("I do think we need to have fire station seven in here"). As President of Methodist Richardson Medical Center since 2010, he runs the hospital's partnership with the Richardson Police Department on the Crisis Intervention Team (mental health crisis co-response). His healthcare/emergency services background, combined with explicit public safety funding advocacy, aligns with answer 4 (increase police and fire staffing, equipment, and pay to improve response times). No evidence of redirecting funds away from police.

Inferred from campaign statements: Hutchenrider identifies economic development as one of Richardson's "largest issues" stating "I want to ensure continued economic development, focus on infrastructure and on neighborhoods." He chairs both the Business Committee and Education Committee on council. His 15-year leadership of Methodist Richardson Medical Center (a $120M expansion under his tenure) reflects his comfort with major institutional investment. Aligns with answer 4 (compete actively for major employers with significant tax abatements and infrastructure investment) — consistent with Richardson's actual incentive-heavy strategy.

As Mayor and former Economic Development Advisory Council chair, Boyles spearheaded aggressive economic-development efforts, courting hundreds of new businesses and promoting El Segundo as having the highest venture funding per square mile, a strongly pro-business-development position.
Boyles paired business growth with "preserving El Segundo's small-town charm" and responsible fiscal management, favoring measured, character-preserving development.

Inferred from budget and city planning: Frisco's FY26 budget allocated road and infrastructure projects as a major spending category, with $50M in infrastructure/road improvements noted. Frisco is a car-dependent DFW suburb with no local bus network or light rail. The "Rail District" redevelopment is a real estate/entertainment district, not a commuter rail project. No record of Cheney advocating for bike lanes, pedestrian networks, or transit expansion as priorities. Value 4: focus on road capacity for the driving majority.

Inferred from public statements: Cheney stated "Texas is very much a property-rights state" and that the city cannot compel developers to offer housing at any particular price. He acknowledged the issue and said the city would "work with businesses to explore viable solutions" but rejected mandates. No record of rent caps, inclusionary zoning requirements, or direct public housing support. Philosophy is to let private market respond to demand. Value 4: cut regulations, let private developers decide.

Livingston represents a council seat in Frisco, a city that has transitioned from boom-growth to a more established suburban community. His housing score reflects skepticism toward new affordable housing mandates or subsidized housing programs that could alter Frisco's predominantly market-rate residential character.

Livingston's maximum zoning score reflects strong opposition to upzoning or density increases in Frisco's established residential areas. Frisco residents have consistently pushed back against apartment and higher-density development as the city has matured, and Livingston has aligned with that constituent sentiment.

Asatryan is a sustained champion of the Beeline transit system, advocating its expansion and full electrification (zero-emissions fleet by 2035); GEC endorsed her specifically for backing "safe and convenient local public transportation especially the BeeLine" plus bicycle/pedestrian safety, and she frames safety around "safer street design, traffic calming... pedestrian protections" — prioritizing transit and active mobility.

GEC endorsed her as "a strong advocate for clean energy" and building electrification, and she backs tree canopy and transit electrification (zero-emissions Beeline by 2035), while stressing clean-energy implementation must be "accessible for all, including renters and small businesses" — a measured invest-in-clean-energy posture rather than emergency bans.

Ortiz's documented economic focus is local businesses and job quality rather than large-employer subsidy competition. He emphasizes supporting locally owned businesses and, as his solution to the district's poverty, bringing in better-paying jobs and providing more workforce training programs. Centering local/small business and higher-quality jobs and training, rather than competing with large tax incentives for major outside employers, aligns with prioritizing small-business support and local entrepreneur/workforce programs.

Ortiz's documented housing priority is affordable access. Representing District 4 — the highest-poverty district in Indio — he has consistently expressed the need for affordable housing options for residents as a central concern. Supporting affordable-housing access and assistance for residents who are priced out, without a documented rent-cap/inclusionary-mandate or a deregulate-for-market-builders mechanism, aligns with offering targeted help such as subsidies and assistance for affordable housing.

McDowell opposes increased environmental regulations to prevent climate change and supports U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Climate Agreement per his iSideWith responses. This aligns with rejecting climate change policies in favor of economic growth, value 5.

McDowell favors expansion of offshore oil drilling and supports drilling in the Alaska Wildlife Refuge per iSideWith responses. He opposes environmental regulations on fossil fuel production. No documented position calling for removal of all environmental restrictions, aligning with value 4 (expand permits).

Opposes raising taxes on wealthy individuals and corporations, supports lowering corporate tax rates, opposes capital gains tax increases, and supports reducing government spending. Favors economic stimulus via tax cuts. Aligns with value 4 (cut taxes for everyone, scale back public services).

Opposes lifting the Social Security earnings cap for high earners, and supports welfare restrictions and spending cuts. No evidence of supporting full privatization. Aligns with value 4 (gradually raise retirement age and reduce benefits for higher earners).

Opposes the ACA and single-payer healthcare, and opposes expanded Medicaid federal funding. He does support pre-existing condition protections and Medicare drug price negotiation, placing him closer to value 4 (help only the poorest, leave others to private insurance) than full privatization.

Opposes expanded Medicaid federal funding and opposes increased federal spending on low-income healthcare. Supports work requirements for Medicaid. Does not support ACA. He supports Medicare drug price negotiation and some targeted protections, placing him at value 4 (partially privatize Medicare, reduce Medicaid coverage) rather than full phase-out.

Opposes birthright citizenship, sanctuary cities, and government services for undocumented immigrants. Supports border wall, deportation enforcement, and reduced immigration from high-risk countries. Voted for Haitian TPS and backed Dreamers, preventing value 5. Aligns with value 4 (make it harder to immigrate legally, limit public services to legal status).

Supports deporting immigrants who commit serious crimes and supports broad border enforcement including wall construction. Voted for Haitian TPS and backed Dreamer status, suggesting he is not at value 5 (deport all immediately regardless of ties). Aligns with value 4 (deport all without legal status, starting with criminal history).
