rows.reasoning: As Massachusetts Secretary of State and chief elections officer, Galvin has been outspoken about combating election misinformation and disinformation. He issued public statements in 2020 and 2022 countering false claims about mail-in voting, ballot security, and election fraud in Massachusetts. His office launched public education campaigns to correct misleading information targeting MA voters. Galvin has called out specific instances of disinformation spread on social media affecting local elections and urged platforms to take action. His long tenure overseeing elections has made election integrity and accurate information central to his public role.

Lewis voted for the 2020 police reform law (Chapter 253) and has been a consistent supporter of criminal justice reform. He has advocated for mental health co-responder programs as alternatives to police for mental health crises and has backed diversion programs for drug offenses. He supported bail reform reducing pretrial detention for non-violent offenses. His approach emphasizes addressing root causes of crime through social services and treatment while supporting community-oriented policing.

Jehlen has been a long-standing champion of reproductive rights. She voted for the 2020 ROE Act expanding abortion access in Massachusetts and removing restrictions including the parental consent requirement for minors. She has backed legislation strengthening protections for abortion providers and patients. After the Dobbs decision she has been outspoken in calling for strengthening Massachusetts as a reproductive healthcare sanctuary and has backed legislation to protect providers and patients from out-of-state prosecution.

Karen E. Spilka has made childcare a signature legislative priority. Under her leadership, the Senate passed the Commonwealth Cares for Children (C3) stabilization grant program, the largest investment in early education in Massachusetts history. She has championed universal pre-K, expanded childcare subsidies, and increased compensation for childcare workers. She has framed high-quality affordable childcare as essential for both families and economic productivity.

Karen E. Spilka championed the VOTES Act under her Senate presidency, permanently establishing early voting, vote-by-mail, and same-day registration in Massachusetts. She prioritized passage of the VOTES Act and signed it with Governor Baker in 2022, calling it historic. She has consistently supported expanding voting access and removing barriers to participation.

Galvin has been a consistent Democratic voice supporting expanded healthcare access throughout his tenure as Secretary of the Commonwealth. Massachusetts was the first state to achieve near-universal healthcare coverage under the 2006 Commonwealth Care law, and Galvin publicly supported its implementation. He has advocated for protecting the Affordable Care Act and maintaining Massachusetts' expanded Medicaid (MassHealth) program. His office issued election-related materials encouraging voter participation in ballot questions affecting healthcare funding, reflecting his support for healthcare access expansion.

Karen E. Spilka has been a healthcare champion as Senate President, prioritizing behavioral health reform, substance use treatment, and mental health parity. Under her leadership, the Senate passed comprehensive behavioral health legislation in 2023, one of the most significant mental health investments in state history. She has also backed Medicaid expansions, maternal health equity, and prescription drug cost reform. She has spoken publicly about her own family's experiences with mental health challenges.

Rodrigues has been the champion of the South Coast Rail project, the multi-decade effort to bring commuter rail service to Fall River and New Bedford. The project was completed and service began in 2023, representing a major transportation victory for his district. As Ways & Means Chairman, he used his budget influence to ensure funding for this project. He has also backed highway improvements in his district and the broader South Coast transportation infrastructure.

Lungo-Koehn oversaw Medford's MBTA Communities Act zoning compliance, creating multifamily overlay districts near the Orange Line and Green Line extension stations. She publicly supported the rezoning to allow denser residential development, stating it was essential to address the regional housing crisis and maintain Medford's eligibility for state housing grants. This put her in favor of relaxing single-family zoning restrictions near transit.

Introduced the concept of a "rat czar" pest management position in 2023 and formally introduced a resolution creating an Office of Pest Control with a dedicated director in January 2024; the council unanimously adopted the ordinance on January 31, 2024. He partnered with Councilor Liz Breadon on the proposal. This represents a proactive government-services approach to sanitation, treating the rat problem as a city services failure requiring dedicated institutional response.

As West Hollywood Mayor, Prang was among California's most vocal marriage equality advocates. When the federal appeals court struck down DOMA in May 2012, he declared: "This puts us one step closer towards equal rights for all Americans. It is just a matter of time before we end, once and for all, this law driven by bigotry." He personally married his partner during the 2008 window before Prop 8 passed and described being "in Sacramento constantly on domestic partnership rights and on marriage equality" during his 13 years on the WeHo council.

Wu's campaign touts that the council under his leadership added 10 police officers ("making our police force 100 strong") and installed the Flock camera system; as mayor his stated public-safety priority is "enhancing resources for police, fire, emergency services." This matches increasing police staffing/equipment to deter crime and improve response (chair 4).

John C. Velis has been a particularly strong champion for veterans' mental health care and has worked on mental health legislation broadly. As a U.S. Army Reserve colonel with overseas deployments, he has led efforts to improve mental health services for veterans and has extended this advocacy to civilian mental health policy. He has backed expanded Medicaid coverage and behavioral health reforms and served as co-chair of the Joint Committee on Mental Health, Substance Use, and Recovery.

As Council President, Krintzman guided Newton's MBTA Communities zoning compliance through the full council process and voted in favor of the plan in October 2023. He has been a persistent voice for increasing housing production and affordability, arguing that Newton must take responsibility for its role in the regional housing crisis. His leadership role gave him an outsized influence on the housing policy agenda.

Laredo has supported a community-policing model and has backed Newton's unarmed mental health co-responder program. He has not advocated for defunding police but has expressed support for diverting some public safety calls to mental health professionals. This is consistent with the progressive-pragmatic approach common among Newton's elected officials.

During the November 2024 special tax session, Miguez publicly broke with Gov. Landry, arguing 'Louisiana has a spending problem' and that spending cuts should precede or accompany the flat income tax cut (HB1 lowering personal income tax to a flat 3%), reflecting a cut-taxes-and-shrink-spending position rather than raising taxes or maintaining the status quo.

Matthews names reparations as a top campaign priority and calls for policy that acknowledges historic injustice, but explicitly limits her proposal to a 'narrowly defined, Tennessee-based policy approach that is fair, transparent, and limited in scope' rather than a sweeping institutional mandate, which best fits the chair favoring stronger civil-rights enforcement and addressing systemic discrimination over either a broad equity mandate or maintaining the status quo.
